<x_0.0156><y_0.0>SWIVEES, a kind of ring made to turn round in a Swinds
flaple, or other ring. Thefe are ufed when a flip lies at her moorings ; alfo in tedders for cattle, that they may turn round without unwarping the tedder.<x_0.8545><y_0.0539><class_Text>

<x_0.0176><y_0.0484>_Swirat-Cannon_, is a fmail piece of artillery belonging to a hip of war, which carries a hot of half a pound, and is fixed in a pocket on the top of the flip's fide, flern, or bow, and alfo in her tops. The trunnions of this piece are contained in a fort of iron crotch, of which the lower end terminates in a cylindrical pivot relating in the pocket, fo as to support the weight of the cannon. The focket is bored in a fitting piece of oak, reinforced with iron hoops, in order to enable it to fuftain the recoil. By means of this frame, which is called the _feuivel_, and an iron handle on its cafcable, the gun may be directed by the hand to any object. It is therefore very necessary in the tops, particularly when loaded with mufket-balls, to fire down on the upper decks of the adversary in action.<x_0.8564><y_0.2437><class_Text>

<x_0.0596><y_0.2398>SWOONING. See MEDICINE, n° 274.<x_0.6553><y_0.2578><class_Section-header>

<x_0.0186><y_0.2531>SWORD, an offensive weapon worn at the fide, and ferving either to cut or flatb. Its parts are, the handle, guard, and blade ; to which may be added the bow, feabbard, pummel, &e.<x_0.8555><y_0.3117><class_Text>

<x_0.0195><y_0.3086>_Sword of State,_ which is borne before the king, lords, and governors of counties, cities, or boroughs, &c. For or before the king, it ought to be carried upright ; the hilt as low as the bearer’s waift, the blade up between his eyes. For or before a duke, the blade mult decline from the head, and be carried between the neck and the right shoulder. For or before an earl, the blade is to be carried between the point of the thoulder and the elbow: and for or before a ba-ron, the blade is to be borne in the bend of the arm. This ceremonial form no lefs denotes the dignity of a governor than the coronet fet on his coat of arms.<x_0.8535><y_0.4609><class_Text>

<x_0.0586><y_0.4586>_Sword-Fijb._ See XIPHIAS.<x_0.46><y_0.4742><class_Section-header>

<x_0.0205><y_0.4719>SWORN BROTHERS (_fratre jurati_), perfons who, by mutual oath, covenanted to fhare each others fortune. For- medly, in any notable expedition to invade and conquer an enemy’s country, it was the cultom for the more eminent fol-diers to engage themselves by reciprocal oaths to fhare the rewards of their service. This practice gave occasion to the proverb of _fworn brothers_ or _brethren in miquity_, because of their dividing plunder and fpoil.<x_0.8525><y_0.5844><class_Text>

<x_0.0605><y_0.582>SYCAMORE-TREE, in botany. See ACER.<x_0.7021><y_0.5977><class_Section-header>

<x_0.0215><y_0.5953>SYCOPHANT, an appellation given by the ancient A-thenians to thofe who informed of the exportation of figs contrary to law; and hence it is fill ufed in general for all informers, parafites, flatterers, cheats, &c.<x_0.8516><y_0.6531><class_Text>

<x_0.0166><y_0.6508>SYDENHAM (Dr Thomas), an excellent English phy-fician, was the fan of William Sydenham of Winford Eagle in Dorfethire, and was born there about the year 1624. He studied at Magdalen-hall, Oxford ; but left that univer-fity when Oxford was garrifoned for king Charles I. and went to London: where, becoming acquainted with Dr Thomas Cox, an eminent physician, that gentleman perfua-ded him to apply himself to the fludy of phyfc ; according-ly, after the garrison was delivered up to the parliament, he retired again to Magdalen-hall, entered on the fludy of medicine, and in 1648 was created bachelor of phyfic. Soon after, he was made a fellow of All-Souls college, and conti-nued there feveral years: when, leaving the univerifty, he fettled at Weftminfter, became doctor of his faculty at Cam-bridge ; grew famous for his practice ; and was the chief phyfician in London from the year 1660 to 1670 ; at which period he began to be dilabled by the gout. He died in 1689. His works are highly eftcemed both at home and abroad.
